FIND: The `section_terminator` regex in `parse_admissibility_block` (line ~109) uses `re.MULTILINE` with `^` anchors, but the `tail` string is a substring of the original `finding_text` starting at an arbitrary offset. The `^` anchor matches the start of the *string*, not the start of a line, when the string does not begin at a line boundary. If the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker is not at the start of a line (e.g., it appears mid-line after some prefix text), `marker_match` will still find it (since the marker regex uses `^` with `re.MULTILINE` on the full `finding_text`), but `tail` will begin mid-line. The subsequent `section_terminator` regex also uses `^` with `re.MULTILINE` on `tail`. If `tail` starts mid-line, the first line of `tail` will not match `^` because `^` only matches after newlines in `re.MULTILINE` mode, not at the start of a string that begins mid-line. This means a section header on the same line as the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker (or immediately after it without a newline) will not be detected as a terminator, causing the block to consume more text than intended.

Concrete example:
```
finding_text = "SOME_PREFIX ADMISSIBILITY:\n  S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."
```
Here `marker_match` finds `ADMISSIBILITY:` at position 12. `tail = finding_text[28:]` = `"\n  S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."`. The `section_terminator` regex with `^` and `re.MULTILINE` will match `NOVELTY:` on the third line because `tail` starts with `\n`, so the first character is a newline and `^` matches after it. This case works.

But consider:
```
finding_text = "ADMISSIBILITY: S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."
```
Here `marker_match` finds `ADMISSIBILITY:` at position 0. `tail = finding_text[14:]` = `" S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."`. The `section_terminator` regex with `^` and `re.MULTILINE` will NOT match `NOVELTY:` because `tail` starts with a space, not a newline, and `^` only matches at string start (which is mid-line) or after newlines. The first line of `tail` is `" S_min: PASS"` — `^` matches at position 0 of `tail`, but `NOVELTY:` is on the second line. Wait — `re.MULTILINE` makes `^` match at the start of the string AND after each newline. So `^NOVELTY` should match at position after `\n`. Let me re-examine.

Actually, `tail = " S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."`. The `^` with `re.MULTILINE` matches at position 0 (start of string) and position 14 (after `\n`). So `^NOVELTY` would match at position 14. This case works.

The real failure case is when the ADMISSIBILITY block content and the next section header are on the same line without a newline separator, or when `tail` starts with content that includes a section header name but not at line start. However, the more significant issue is:

If `finding_text` contains `ADMISSIBILITY:` at the very end of the string with no trailing newline, `tail` is empty string `""`. Then `section_terminator` returns `None`, `block = tail` (empty string), and all gates fail — which is correct behaviour (missing block = all gates fail).

The actual bug is subtler: the `section_terminator` regex uses `^\s*` which requires the section name to be at the start of a line. But the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker regex also uses `^\s*`. If the input text has the ADMISSIBILITY block indented (e.g., inside a markdown code block or quoted text), both regexes will fail to match because `^` matches start of line, and indented text has leading whitespace that `^\s*` handles. Wait — `^\s*` DOES handle leading whitespace. So indentation is fine.

The actual edge case: if the ADMISSIBILITY block is followed immediately by another section on the same line (no newline), e.g.:

The `σ_measured` gate treats N/A as equivalent to PASS. But per §15, `σ_measured` requires a pre/post measurement pair. N/A means "not applicable" (e.g., no fix was proposed). Treating N/A as PASS means a finding that proposes no fix and correctly reports σ_measured as N/A will have that gate marked as passed, which is semantically wrong — the gate is not passed, it's not applicable. FINDING_ID: F004

FIND: The `section_terminator` regex includes `FINDING` as a terminator, but this is overly aggressive. The field name is `FINDING_ID`, not `FINDING`. If a model writes `FINDING` as a standalone word in the ADMISSIBILITY evidence text (e.g., "evidence=see FINDING above" or "this FINDING is novel"), the parser will incorrectly terminate the ADMISSIBILITY block at that point, truncating the block and potentially missing subsequent gate declarations. The `FINDING` terminator was likely added as a catch-all alongside `FINDING_ID`, but it creates a false-positive termination risk.

Concrete example:
```
ADMISSIBILITY:
  S_min: PASS (location=bench/foo.py:42, mechanism=off-by-one, evidence=this FINDING is documented in test_case_7)
  G-completeness: PASS
```
Here `FINDING` appears in the S_min evidence text. The `section_terminator` regex matches `FINDING` followed by `\s*:`, but in this case `FINDING` is followed by ` is documented...`, not `:`. Wait — the regex requires `\s*:` after the section name. So `FINDING is` would NOT match because there's no `:` after `FINDING`. The regex is `FINDING\s*:`, which requires a colon. So `FINDING:` would match, but `FINDING ` (without colon) would not.

But what if a model writes `FINDING:` in the evidence text? E.g., `evidence=see FINDING: the off-by-one error`. This would incorrectly terminate the block. This is a real risk, though mitigated by the fact that `FINDING:` is unlikely to appear in natural-language evidence text (models typically write `FINDING_ID: F001` not `FINDING: something`).

The more realistic risk: `FIND` is also in the terminator list. The word "find" is common in English. If evidence text contains "find:" (e.g., "we find: the bug is..."), the block terminates prematurely. This is a higher risk than `FINDING:`.

FOLLOW: Premature termination of the ADMISSIBILITY block causes gates declared after the false terminator to be treated as missing, marking them as FAIL. This produces false-negative admissibility verdicts, which feed into the feedback channel and incorrectly flag valid findings as inadmissible.

ANALYSE: SOFT constraint. The parser is documented as "deliberately simple" and "format-strict rejection lives downstream." False terminations are a known risk of regex-based parsing. However, the inclusion of `FIND` as a terminator is particularly risky given its frequency in English text. CONFIRMED.
